Review: MXenes for energy storage and conversion 
devices—advances in green synthesis, use 
of machine‑learning, and electrochemical response
Anthony Chukwunonso Opia1,2,* , Kumaran Kadirgama1,2,*, Stanley C. Mamah1, 
Mohd Fairusham Ghazali1, Wan Sharuzi Wan Harun2, Agi Augustine1, and Alibi Sylvanus3
1 Centre for Research in Advanced Fluid and Processes, Universiti Malaysia Pahang Al-Sultan Abdullah, Pekan, Malaysia

ABSTRACT
Recently, MXenes have become effective electrode materials for devices including 
batteries, supercapacitors (SCs), sensors, antennas, and optoelectronic devices, as 
well as for sustainable energy storage. They are promising choices for a variety of 
energy conversion and storage materials due to their metallic conductivity, good 
hydrophilicity, and ability to act as ideal templates for developing other materi-
als with tunable features. Recent advances in energy devices and storage using 
MXene as electrode materials are outlined in this article. The fundamental ideas 
of energy storage and renovation systems are examined. The following sections 
highlight the special qualities of Green Synthesis Methods for MXenes. Potential 
fixes for issues that arose during the development of MXene were investigated, as 
was the use of Machine learning techniques as cutting-edge approaches to MXene 
product optimisation. Additionally, MXene’s applications in energy conversion 
devices, such as supercapacitors, catalysis, various batteries, and electrochemi-
cal sensing were highlighted. A discussion of potential future opportunities for 
MXene-based materials in energy industries for sustainable technology wraps 
up the study.
Introduction

greater focus is being placed on the research and appli-
cation of renewable energy sources, such as solar and 
wind power, due to their potential towards reducing 
pollution. However, the intermittent nature of different 
energy sources necessitates the development of effec-
tive systems for energy conversion and storage since 
energy is essential to modern life and fuels our homes,

36]. The MXene structure’s transition metal layer 
count is determined by the value of n [37 , 38]. Every 
element of MXenes metals, atoms, numbers, functional 
groups, etc. (M, X, n, and Tx) is essential to defining its 
characteristics. The number of metal layers in MXenes 
can vary from 2 in M2XTx structures to 5 in  M5X4Tx 
structures [39].
The interlayer spacing, which is influenced by 
the number of metals layers, has an impact on the 
mechanical properties of MXenes, ion transport 
kinetics, and the accessibility of active sites for elec -
trochemical reactions [40, 41]. Researchers can con-
trol characteristics including mechanical strength, 
surface chemistry, electrical conductivity, thermal 
stability, and electrochemical performance by adjust-
ing the composition and layer arrangement of MXenes 
[42–47]. There has been a notable advancement in the 
synthesis of different kinds of MXenes since the first

of interest [36, 50].  Ti2C3Tx [51, 52],  Nb2CTx,  Ti3C2Tx/
Fe2O3,  Ti3C2Tx/TiO2 [53, 54],  Cr2TiC2Tx,   V2CTx [55], and 
 V4C3Tx are a few MX-based materials that have been 
documented for energy storage/conversion applica-
tions [56, 57]. According to research, both Titanium 
[20, 58], Niobium, Chromium and Vanadium-based 
MXenes [15, 59], for instance, have demonstrated out-
standing electrochemical performance, putting them 
promising candidates for energy storage/conversion 
applications [1, 3, 12, 60]. There are currently over 50 
MXenes with diverse transition metals (M) and surface 
terminations (Tx) depending on the elements, some 
of which are shown in Fig. 2, with their documented 
works from 2018 to 2025. The information was gen-
erated by merging the keywords; MXene additives, 
energy storage, and conversion in the ISI Web of Sci-

The findings revealed that of all the MXenes-based 
materials reviewed,  Ti2CTx,  Ti2C2Tx, and  TiC2Tx/Fe2O3

cal advancements [1–3]. Electrochemical energy tech-
nologies, such as electrocatalytic water-splitting, Li-ion 
batteries (LIBs), non-Li-ion batteries, and Supercapaci-
tors (SCs), have been seen as viable renewable energy 
sources [4 –6]. Access to affordable, reliable energy 
supplies puts a nation in a better position to attract 
foreign capital, create opportunities, and achieve sus-
tained economic growth [4 , 7]. Nevertheless, these 
devices’ present performance is insufficient to satisfy 
the growing need for large-scale energy storage [8–11]. 
It is critical to investigate and identify novel materials 
with improved performance for energy storage/con-
version systems to overcome this obstacle.
Experts have been exploring materials that can pro-
vide better energy conversion and storage capabilities. 
These cutting-edge materials may enable the creation 
of more reliable and efficient energy storage devices, 
easing the grid’s transition to renewable energy 
sources and reducing reliance on fossil fuels [1–3, 12]. 
In this concept, many studies have been conducted on 
new electrode materials [13, 14], electrolytes [11, 15], 
and storage/conversion devices [16, 17] for household 
and industrial applications. Since the ground-breaking 
discovery of graphene [18, 19], interest in studying dif-
ferent two-dimensional (2D) materials has increased 
dramatically. These two-dimensional materials dem-
onstrated superior chemical and physical characteris-
tics. These inspired the synthesis and investigation of 
numerous other atomic-layer materials for a variety 
of uses, including silicene, germanane, phosphorene, 
hexagonal boron nitride (h-BN) [16, 20], and transition 
metal dichalcogenides (TMDs) [21– 23]. These materi-
als are all appealing for scientific study and potential 
uses due to their distinct qualities and traits [23, 24]. 
The large surface area-to-volume ratio and the interior 
surface area of 2D materials are noteworthy advan-
tages that make them attractive options for energy 
storage and conversion devices [25–27].
In recent years, the field of engineering has become 
interested in a unique family of 2D materials called 
MXenes due to their physiochemical properties [13, 14, 
28] (high hydrophilicity, flexibility, diversity, chemi-
cal stability, electrical conductivity, and alterable sur-
face chemistry). These made them attractive options 
for a range of uses, especially energy storage and 
converters [1 , 2]. As presented in Fig. 1, MXenes are 
made from a type of 3D material called MAX phases 
[29, 30], revealing the various phases under different

Machine learning technique for MXene 
optimisation
To overcome the drawbacks of conventional mate -
rial design and synthesis techniques for MXenes, 
Machine learning (ML) is essential. This provides a 
mechanism to expedite study and innovation in this 
area [94, 95]. ML algorithms are excellent at handling 
complex datasets and analysing vast amounts of 
data, providing insights that traditional approaches 
might find difficult to obtain. Through finding 
designs and connections in experimental and com-
putational information, Machine learning can help 
decipher complex surface chemistry in the instance 
of MXenes [96]. This enables the design of MXenes 
with specific features by allowing researchers to clar-
ify the connections between MXene attributes and 
different synthesis conditions [97]. Predicting and 
improving MXene properties, particularly thickness 
estimation, is made possible in large part by Machine 
learning methods.
ML can improve the precision of MXene layer 
thickness prediction by training models on a variety 
of datasets, including computational simulations, 
experimental thickness measurements, and other 
pertinent characteristics [95]. This addresses a sig-
nificant drawback of conventional methods and ena-
bles efficient synthesis of MXenes with the desired 
mechanical and electrical properties. The investiga-
tion of dynamic phenomena in MXenes is aided by 
Machine learning. According to Rosenkranz et al. 
[98], time-dependent data can be analysed using 
ML algorithms to identify patterns and variations in 
MXene structures under diverse conditions. ML ena-
bles the creation of predictive replicas for more effec-
tive production processes, thereby improving scal-
ability and optimising synthesis. ML algorithms can 
recommend optimal settings for scalable, repeatable 
MXene synthesis by evaluating synthesis conditions 
and results across multiple experiments, thereby 
speeding up large-scale manufacturing efforts [99, 
100].

ML methods
Large datasets and machine learning applications 
allow computers to learn and adapt, removing many 
programming hazards and dead ends. These algo-
rithms can recognise trends, draw conclusions from 
training data, and adapt over time. Various Machine 
learning techniques are used in the literature to assess 
risk. "Machine learning," a branch of computer science, 
seeks to learn from data to advance operations across 
a variety of tasks [101]. Figure 6 lists the different 
approaches used in Machine learning operations. By 
employing recent research tools and data to forecast 
various material properties, ML techniques have been 
used in numerous fields to accelerate the data-collec-
tion process.
ML techniques may assist at all stages of the MXene 
process, including constituent design, synthesis, and 
the discovery of new MXene structures. This enables 
rapid discovery of viable candidates and the best 
processing conditions to achieve the required mate-
rial attributes. With projecting practice in the design 
and synthesis of efficient materials, such as MXenes, 
ML is a powerful tool in materials research [103]. The 
following are some important domains in which ML 
techniques are applied in MXene characterisation:
(a) Materials quality Prediction: Researchers can find 
MXenes with desirable qualities for particular 
applications by using ML models [95] to predict 
a variety of material features of MXenes, includ-
ing electronic band assemblies, mechanical and 
thermal characteristics.
(b) Improved Finding: By recommending composi-
tions and structures that are possible to display 
desired features, machine learning techniques 
facilitate the quick run of possible MXene grade 
from a large chemical space, which also speeds up 
the materials detection process [95].
(c) Structure-feature Interactions: ML aids in the 
development of intricate connections between 
MXenes’ structural characteristics and their 
attributes [104], which makes it easier to design 
MXenes with optimal performance for particular 
uses.
(d) Synthesis Optimisation: To improve the circum-
stances for the production of MXene, Machine 
learning algorithms can examine data from exper-
imental procedures. Predicting optimal synthesis 
features, such as temperature, precursor ratios, 
and reaction duration, is part of this [105].
(e) Finding New MXene Compositions: To find 
trends and suggest new compositions or struc -
tures that haven’t been investigated, Machine 
learning methods are used to analyse current 
MXene databases and literature [106].
(f) Property-centred Material Design: Through con-
sidering several attributes at once, machine learn-
ing algorithms enable a data-driven approach to 
material design [107]. This aids researchers in 
optimising MXene compositions for a variety of

As presented, the current data-driven materials 
paradigm, which uses ML, improved characterisation, 
and experimental synthesis in a continuous feedback 
loop to speed up materials discovery and optimisation, 
is reflected in this roadmap. This approach reduces 
trial-and-error experiments, lowers development cost, 
shortens material discovery time, and enables faster 
optimisation of high-performance materials for energy 
storage applications.
Data‑driven methods and density functional 
theory (DFT) replicas
Due to their poor computational scaling, electronic 
structure approaches present difficulties. Large-scale 
simulations involving more than a few thousand 
atoms require significant time and computational 
effort. Data-driven processes offer a solution, adding 
or replacing traditional DFT calculations to accelerate 
calculations [109]. The compilation of vast amounts of 
theoretical and experimental data across a wide range 
of knowledge disciplines has increased dramatically 
during the past three decades. The success of DFT 
and the rapid increase in computational power are 
primarily responsible for the vast amount of data in 
computational materials research [ 110]. At the same 
time, advancements in electronics and instrumentation 
have enabled experiments to produce large volumes 
of data. This establishes the groundwork for the crea-
tion of novel instruments that can extract information 
from theoretical and experimental databases [111]. 
The main force behind the several Machine learning 
techniques used in current research and development 
is the field of statistical learning. Two theorems that 
describe the structure and properties of organic mate-
rials, such as MXenes, form the foundation of DFT and 
have been elaborated [112]. These theorems show that: 
(i) the electronic density m(r) is the only factor that 
may define the external potential on electrons in a sys-
tem with MMM electrons; and (ii) the ground-state 
energy EG[m] reaches its minimal value for the precise 
electronic density [113].
The mathematical expression for these theorems 
is expressed in Eq. 8. As stated in Eq. 9, the external 
potential is regarded as a functional of the ground-
state density.
Considering that some of the functionals’ forms are 
already known, where Vext is known to be an external 
potential, Ts is the Kohn–Sham kinetic energy, and 
UH stands for the Hartree potential. The Kohn-Sham 
kinetic energy is given by Eq. 10 for the non-inter-
acting orientation system [114]. Equations  11 and 12 
are resolved to generate the known Kohn–Sham (KS) 
Eq. 13 [114].
This set of equations describes a self-consistent 
cycle in which fj denotes the Lagrange multipliers, 
commonly interpreted as the energy levels of the 
Kohn–Sham orbitals. One begins with a tentative 
density m(r), incorporates an efficient form of vxc, and 
constructs the effective potential veff. The electronic 
density is then calculated from the set of fj eigenvector 
values, and the process is repeated until convergence 
criteria, usually based on the system’s total energy, 
are met.

Using convolutional neural network models (CNN) 
and random forest (RF), Haider et al. [116] recently 
predicted the heat of production of numerous MXene 
materials. Using 12 distinct MXenes properties, the 
neural network model predicts the heat of formation 
with a mean absolute error (MAE) of 0.18 eV for train-
ing data and 0.21 eV for testing data. According to 
this study [116], the CNN model outstripped the RF 
models. ML represents a paradigm shift in materials 
research when coupled with first-principles ab initio 
calculations. Ab initio methods like DFT, which solve 
quantum-mechanical equations to predict material 
properties with high accuracy, are crucial for under-
standing the fundamental behaviour of materials 
[117]. Understanding how different parameters affect 
MXenes’ thermodynamic favourability and stability 
in a range of applications is crucial. However, these 
approaches are time-consuming and computationally 
challenging, especially for large or complicated sys -
tems. By leveraging the benefits of both approaches, 
the drive to replace or enhance DFT significantly nar-
rows the search space for novel materials, enabling 
the training of fast, scalable algorithms using working-
based descriptors [118].
MXenes surface functionalization, 
constituents, and structure prediction using 
machine learning models
These models are essential for forecasting MXene 
surface functionalisation, composition, and shape, 
as they provide insightful information and acceler-
ate the discovery of new materials [119]. Current data 
on MXenes and their functionalisation processes can 
be used to create ML models that can replicate and 
modify patterns [120]. Machine learning algorithms 
can predict the likely functional groups bound to the 
MXene surface by analysing experimental results and 
factors such as temperature, reaction duration, and 
inhibitor concentrations. Customising surface charac-
teristics for specialised applications, such as catalysis 
or sensing, is particularly helpful. The ideal conditions 
for effectively achieving desired surface alterations can 
be predicted by analysing a range of experimental 
parameters [119].
Using a variety of input characteristics, such as pre-
cursor materials, reaction conditions, and synthesis 
techniques, Machine learning models predict MXene 
composition [106]. Considering the required mechani-
cal, optical, or electrical properties helps researchers 
identify appropriate compositions for specific applica-
tions. When MXenes have multi-layer or components, 
ML models can forecast the composition of each layer, 
aiding understanding of the intricate structure and its 
effects on the material’s characteristics. To anticipate 
MXene properties, ML algorithms can examine data 
on synthesis techniques, precursor characteristics, 
and experimental setups. This is necessary to modify 
MXene’s morphology for certain applications, such 
as catalysis or energy storage. Additionally, by learn-
ing from a dataset of experimental results, Machine 
learning-driven optimisation proposes formulation 
settings that produce MXenes with specific morpholo-
gies [121].
ML application on electronic band 
morphology, thermo‑mechanical properties, 
and catalytic activity
Computational techniques effectively evaluate exper-
imental data and convert it into useful information. 
This computer data analysis greatly increases the 
accuracy of analysis and description while reducing 
the possibility of artificial misinterpretation [122]. Pre-
dicting material properties, discovering and develop-
ing novel materials, and achieving other goals are the 
three main areas in which Machine learning is used 
in materials science. Machine learning techniques use 
regression analysis methods to predict material prop-
erties at both the macroscopic and microscopic levels 
[123]. To find and create new materials, Machine learn-
ing techniques build probabilistic models to explore 
possible combinations of structures and compositions. 
After sorting through the various combinations, the 
algorithm chooses materials with the required char-
acteristics and functionality. The selected material 
is then validated using DFT-based techniques. ML 
is useful for additional material science goals, such
